en: Finding no place to pitch camp in full strength,
Finding no hero to relieve his cares,
Finding no land to settle in full force,
Finding no lion who would know his worth,
He roamed the face of the land,
Searching it, leaving no spring aside.
Steed-like Manas, the leopard,
Your saint born to perfection,
A follower of twelve spiritual guides,
Created with surpassing fortune—
The dervish named Kydyr
Himself accompanied him and opened his way.
His majesty was fearsome, his wrath was mighty;
Such was your elder's nature:
Whoever clashed with him, he leveled flat.
His figure and his bearing—
That worthy hero of surpassing fortune—
His appearance surpassed other mortals.
His face was like wheat rubbed with oil,
His eyes were like the twilight mist.
His father Jakyp had been driven away,
Wandering, unable to find a way,
Grieving, surviving humiliation.
His brothers had numbered eight;
Grieving that he could find none,
Spending nights in humiliation,
Spending days in humiliation,
He went and made Altai his home,
And those called Manchus and Kalmyks
He mingled with and made his people.
From wealthy Jakyp himself
Wolf-maned Manas was born.
When he reached the age of twelve,
He killed those who challenged him
And brought tumult upon the Kalmyks.
His valor became known to the people;
“He is a bloodthirsty Burut,” they said.
When he reached the age of twelve,
Esenkan, the khan of Beijing,
Had him inscribed in his register.
He himself was born in Altai;
Breaking a court and taking spoils,
Upon the Black Kalmyks of Altai
He had brought tumult.
When he charged, he could not have his fill of blood;
He spared none who fought him.
He unleashed a terrible fury,
Laying flat those who challenged him,
He slaughtered them to the last.
He skirted the mountains of Altai;
Those who said, “I will bind him,”
Your falcon, whom Kydyr had visited,
Burned them all, leaving not one.
Dust rose from his passing;
The Chinese who challenged him were beaten;
Souls fled at the sound of his voice.
Your bloodthirsty hero himself—
A champion who grappled had surpassed him.
Of all who challenged him,
The bloodthirsty hero spilled their blood.
To the Chinese under their kakan
His fighting became known.
“He is a bloodthirsty Burut,” they said;
In the register of Beijing's Karykan
He was inscribed.
He brought disaster upon them;
All those whom he encountered,
He smashed to fragments,
He utterly overcame;
The Kyrgyz had their fill of spoils.
Of the Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
Khan Baltay feared their people:
“They will bring us all to our end;
If those deeply rooted swine sweep upon us,
They may unexpectedly take Manas,
Bind him and carry him off alive.
They will wreak many dreadful things;
Manas, on whom we rely,
They will bring him to his death.
Amid the many seething Chinese
We dwell.
When this Manas was not here,
The many seething Chinese
Used to wreak many dreadful things,
Beating us to ruin, using force,
They counted out and took their dues.
When this Manas was not here,
They made us toil bent over, extracting salt.
‘They are needed by the kakan,’ they said,
And took away many skilled craftswomen.
Manas arose for their good fortune—
They had been committing oppression.
He scattered the Chinese livestock, they said,
Making the Kyrgyz very rich,
He opened their eyes, tiny as flour pellets, they said.
Manas was born for good fortune;
He brought tumult upon the Kalmyks.
Akbaltay was a wise man;
He pressed Manas hard with his words,
Saying, ‘Your descent is Kyrgyz.’
The one word Akbaltay spoke
Was a sullied word lodged in his breast.
‘Ala-Too is your land,’ he said,
‘Those Kyrgyz are your people,’ he said.
Hearing the wise khan's words,
Hearing, ‘Your far-flung kin are Kyrgyz,’
Akbaltay spoke plainly:
‘Khan Koshoy of the Katagan
Will be your falcon,’ he said.
‘He is the hero who will find what suits you,
He is the lion who will understand your full strength.
Your elder Koshoy is an outstanding khan;
He is a man you can lean upon.
He is the khan of the Katagan,
He is a man of sacred power.’”
Those were the words Akbaltay spoke:
“Your elder, old Koshoy—
Be sure to meet him,” he had said.
“To Koshoy, the great khan who is our support,
Let me go and offer greetings;
My elder, champion Koshoy,
Let me come face to face with him.
Chewing white wheat flour together,
Holding the holy Quran together,
With stars in heaven turning pale,
Becoming friends into the afterlife,
Let me seek Koshoy's counsel;
My aged elder Koshoy,
Let me take him as my support.
If we fight, from the Black Chinese
Let me take my unavenged revenge.
The Kalmyks who are in Altai,
Let me drive and chase them to Khangai.
The Black Chinese who fight us—
If Khan Koshoy is my support,
Let me chase them all the way to Beijing.
My champion elder Koshoy,
Let me bind him about my waist as support.
Holding a spear, breaking their ranks,
Falling to a bullet if fate decrees,
Let me bring slaughter upon the peoples.
To this dear elder of mine, Koshoy,
Let me go to see him face to face.”
The bloodthirsty lion spoke these words:
“I shall go to Koshoy now.”
The lord set forth and took the road.
That day Manas traveled on,
Traveled far, not sparing his horse.
When noon had tilted and passed,
Crossing uneven mountains,
Traversing ridges up and down,
Hero Manas grew eager.
Along At-Bashy,
To your elder, old Koshoy,
To the palace with its gateway,
Along Chech-Töbö,
In great Koshoy's fortress,
In the marshes of Keng-Özön,
The Kyrgyz lay settled at ease.
It was a ridge of rolling hills;
They called it Father Chech-Töbö.
On the hills were mottled-headed horses;
In hero Koshoy's keeping
Argymaks and fleet steeds mingled.
Summering at Chech-Töbö,
Hero Koshoy, who knew no measure,
Had tethered his tulpars.
Wearing a sable hat to match,
It was his time to sway at ease.
Letting no one rule over his head,
Your elder Koshoy at that time
Was living in happiness.
Such was Koshoy's condition:
That precious land of Zheti-Özön—
He skillfully made it his country;
The Kyrgyz in Zheti-Özön
He managed to make into a people.
Your elder, old Koshoy,
Was a saint unlike other men.
His blessing enriched the nation,
An elder in the likeness of a prophet.
From being poor, he grew rich;
From being alone, he grew numerous.
He gathered harriers and made them hunting hawks,
Gathered disparate folk and made them a nation.
He trained a stray bird into a hunting hawk,
Gathered wanderers and made them a nation.
Your elder Koshoy, an outstanding hero,
Was a sage, a cultivator of wisdom.
None who met him went empty-handed,
No enemy made him bow.
Your elder, old Koshoy,
No enemy overcame him face to face;
No man dared approach him in defiance.
He was that hero, leopard Koshoy.
He entered the caliph's presence and received a letter,
He received a blessing from a prince;
He became a disciple of twelve spiritual guides,
And he was called the Illustrious One.
Wherever he went, he made a town;
Of the enemies who fought him,
How many he brought to ruin!
A champion in combat, a hero at jousting,
Hero Koshoy was a marksman at shooting.
Never drawing back from death,
Never retreating from a foe he faced,
Kudaynazar the bare club
Was old Koshoy's companion.
His hearing ear, his seeing eye,
He was your elder Koshoy's trusted man.
Broad-jawed and broad-tongued,
Kutunay in his pale felt hat
Was old Koshoy's fellow in counsel.
His scout was Chalybay,
Soft as dough of white wheat,
Lion Koshoy's sworn friend.
Calling those of his court,
Koshoy had first dreamed a dream,
And seen good things befall him.
Those learned in interpreting dreams,
All those whose ears heard far,
Hero Koshoy had gathered,
The elders who had seen much,
The wise men and the eloquent;
Gathering the people to deliberate,
Koshoy, skilled in custom, held a feast
And had his dream interpreted then.
Of fat stock, beginning with a mare,
Your champion Koshoy ordered slaughter.
Breaking off sugar white as snow,
Cutting chunks of clarified butter,
A fat lamb, a sweet-tasting head,
Suckling camel calves and yearlings together,
He had them put in together, they say,
And had bor boiled, they say.
To have the dream he saw interpreted,
Khan Koshoy began to speak, they say.
“From spearmen to the wise,
Your able men stand here.
We were a Kyrgyz people of diverse kinds;
Your finest men stand here!
We made Chech-Töbö our home;
Fighting how many enemies,
We made a few households into a people.
Lying at night, I dreamed a dream:
I had girded on an unsheathed sword;
When I brandished it toward the sunrise,
It set the east on fire.
Many crows flew in a seething swarm,
But they could not reach that sword.
Kara-Too, stretching across the way,
Split in two when it struck.
That very Kara-Too
Was split in two by the steel.
What kind of dream could this be?
Interpret this dream of mine!
